1002.title: Zheng He
1002.hook: the Muslim admiral of the Ming dynasty who sailed as far as East Africa
1002.howItsDone: Zheng He is remembered in China as a great navigator, by Hui Muslims as one of their own, and in Southeast Asia at shrines and temples, such as Sam Po Kong in Semarang on Java, that bear his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Xi'an's Great Mosque, with a pagoda for a minaret and courtyards facing west: a mosque in Chinese dress.

A giraffe walks into the court of the emperor of China. Long neck, patterned coat, gentle eyes, swaying above officials in silk robes. Nobody at court quite knows what it is. Some decide it must be a qilin, a creature of legend that appears only when the world is ruled well. The giraffe had come a very long way, from Africa, in the years when a great Chinese fleet was sailing those seas. And the fleet's commander was a Muslim from the far southwest of China. Today: Zheng He.
screen: `A GIRAFFE AT THE EMPEROR'S COURT.` → `A CREATURE OF LEGEND?` → `CARRIED BY A CHINESE FLEET.`

segments.voice: Zheng He was born Ma He, in Yunnan, into a Muslim family. A stone inscription for his father calls him hajji, one who had made the pilgrimage to Mecca. As a boy, Ma He was captured when the armies of the new Ming dynasty took Yunnan, and he was taken into the household of a prince. He rose, and became the prince's trusted servant. When that prince became the Yongle emperor, the boy from Yunnan, now named Zheng He, became admiral of great fleets sent across the Indian Ocean. They called at Java and Malacca, at Sri Lanka and the coast of India, at Hormuz in the Gulf, at ports of Arabia, and as far as the coast of East Africa. They carried silk and porcelain, envoys and gifts, and sailed home with ambassadors, spices and gifts, among them, from envoys, giraffes. His Muslim interpreter, Ma Huan, wrote down what they saw in each land. Zheng He sailed for an empire, not as a missionary; the voyages were about trade, power and prestige. But in ports from Java to Arabia he would have met Muslim communities who prayed as his family prayed. The Qur'an says God has honored the children of Adam, and carries them on the land and the sea. In Java, temples and shrines still remember his name. And here the journey through East and Southeast Asia ends: from traders on the straits to an admiral on the open ocean.

1003.title: The art of calligraphy
1003.hook: writing Allah's words beautifully became the highest art
1003.howItsDone: Muslim calligraphers train under a master, write with a cut reed pen, and receive an ijaza when ready; their work fills mosque walls, Qur'an pages and framed panels in Muslim homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zheng He, the admiral, and a giraffe at the emperor's court. That closed the voyage through East and Southeast Asia.

A reed, dried and hard, about the length of a hand. A small knife. The calligrapher holds the reed against a block of bone, cuts the tip at a slant, then splits it with one careful stroke. The ink is dark and thick. The paper has been polished smooth. Before the first letter, a long pause. Then the reed moves, and a single line swells and thins like a breath. A new stretch of the path begins here, the arts, and it begins with a line. Today's word: khatt.
screen: `A REED, A KNIFE, A SLANTED CUT.` → `A LONG PAUSE, THEN ONE STROKE.` → `A NEW PART: THE ARTS.`

segments.voice: Khatt is Arabic for a line, and for handwriting, and so for the art of beautiful writing: calligraphy. Why did writing, of all things, become so central to Islamic art? Start with the Qur'an. Muslims believe it is the speech of God, revealed in Arabic. One surah opens with an oath on the pen itself: "Nun. By the pen and that which they write." A scripture that swears by the pen gives the pen weight. So copying the Qur'an became an act of devotion, and doing it beautifully a way of honoring the words. Calligraphers trained for years under a master. Letters were measured in dots made by the tip of the pen, so every alif and every curve kept its proportion. When a student was ready, the master gave a written license, an ijaza, to sign their own work. It names the teacher, and often the teacher's teacher, so each new calligrapher stands in a chain of hands. In the tradition's own telling, calligraphy came to stand above the other arts. Stand before a mosque wall and you can see why: the words are the decoration. Not a picture of something holy. The holy words themselves, made beautiful. Beautiful writing.

segments.voice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper, and write bismillah, "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful," in Arabic if you know it, in English, or just the one word. Go slower than feels normal, one stroke to one breath, then write it once more without judging the first. If you are Muslim, you may say it as you write.

1004.title: Kufic, Naskh, Thuluth
1004.hook: angular, round, grand: the main scripts
1004.howItsDone: Calligraphers learn the classical scripts one by one under a master, using Naskh for readable texts and Thuluth for large panels and inscriptions, while Kufic and square Kufic appear in carving, tilework and brick.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khatt, the art of the reed pen, and a mosque wall where the words are the decoration.

Say your own name three ways. First as a sergeant would bark it across a parade ground: clipped, square, every edge hard. Then the way a friend says it across the kitchen table: easy, round, clear. Then the way an announcer calls it into a stadium: long, rising, filling the whole space. Same name, three voices. Arabic calligraphy works like that. The same holy words can be written in different scripts, and each one speaks in its own voice. Today: Kufic, Naskh and Thuluth.
screen: `ONE NAME, THREE WAYS.` → `CLIPPED, ROUND, RISING.` → `SAME WORDS, THREE VOICES.`

segments.voice: Kufic first. Its name, tradition says, comes from the city of Kufa in Iraq. Kufic is angular: straight strokes, sharp corners, letters stretched long along the line. It looks carved even in ink, and it carves beautifully, into stone, into wood, into the borders of buildings. Builders even laid it out in bricks and tiles as square Kufic, the letters turned into a maze of right angles, so a wall could spell a name of God over and over. Kufic is the voice of the inscription: firm, monumental, a little stern. Naskh is the friend at the table. Its letters are rounded and even, small clear shapes the eye reads quickly. It became a script for books, for copying the Qur'an to be read. Naskh wants to be understood. Thuluth is the announcer. Tall uprights, wide sweeping curves, letters that climb over one another and interlace, often stacked in layers. It's written large, for the headings of Qur'an chapters and across the walls and domes of mosques, meant to be seen from below and far away. So take one short line: "Say: He is Allah, the One!" In Kufic it stands like a gate. In Naskh it reads like a letter. In Thuluth it rises like a call. Each script a voice.
screen: `KUFIC: ANGULAR, CARVED, FIRM.` · `SQUARE KUFIC: A MAZE OF BRICKS.` · `NASKH: ROUND AND CLEAR, FOR READING.` · `THULUTH: TALL, SWEEPING, FOR WALLS.` · then, large: `EACH SCRIPT A VOICE.`

segments.voice: Write one short word, your own name if you like, in straight lines only, all corners and no curves, like Kufic. Then write it again, round and easy, like Naskh, and set the two side by side. Which one sounds louder, which one kinder, and which would you carve over a door?
Kufic. The angular script, tradition says named for Kufa, carved in stone and built in bricks. Beside it, Naskh, round, and Thuluth, grand. Today's word.
Your line: each script a voice. Same words, a different way of standing on the page. Until tomorrow.

1005.title: Why no figures in mosques
1005.hook: mosques avoid images of living beings, so pattern and word fill the walls
1005.howItsDone: Mosques are decorated with calligraphy, geometric patterns and plant designs rather than images of people or animals; Muslim scholars differ on pictures outside the mosque, and some Muslim lands have long traditions of painted manuscripts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kufic, Naskh and Thuluth: angular, round and grand. Each script a voice.

A small child, maybe on a first visit to a big mosque, tugs a parent's sleeve and whispers: where are the pictures? It's a fair question. The walls are covered, floor to ceiling. Tiles in blue and white. Stars inside stars. Vines curling into vines. Lines of Arabic running around the dome. But no faces. No saints, no prophets, no animals, no people at all. Every inch decorated, and not one living creature in sight. Today: image-makers.
screen: `WHERE ARE THE PICTURES?` → `EVERY INCH DECORATED.` → `NOT ONE LIVING CREATURE.`

segments.voice: Start with God. The Qur'an says of Him: "Naught is as His likeness." Muslims take that to mean nothing in creation can picture God, so a mosque never tries. Then the prophets: Muslims honor them, and a mosque doesn't paint them on its walls to be gazed at in prayer. Then the hadith. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, warns sternly against image-makers, who on the Day of Judgment are told to breathe life into what they made, and cannot. Another report says angels don't enter a house where there are pictures. And there's a very human story, also in Bukhari. A man who made his living painting pictures came to Ibn Abbas, a companion of the Prophet, worried about his work. Ibn Abbas told him the warning, then gave him a way through: if you must paint, paint trees, and things that have no soul. Scholars read these reports in different ways. Some hold that every image of a living being is forbidden. Others say the concern is statues, or images that could be worshiped, and allow pictures in books or homes. And some Muslim lands, such as Persia and Mughal India, have rich traditions of painted figures in manuscripts and palaces. But the mosque, the place of prayer, keeps the figures out. So what fills the walls? The word, as in calligraphy. And pattern: stars, vines, interlacing lines that never settle on one creature to look at. The eye keeps moving, past the tile, past the wall. Pattern points past itself.

segments.voice: Let your eyes move slowly around wherever you are, a tiled floor, the weave of a sweater, bricks, leaves outside, until you find one pattern to stay with. Follow it to its edge, and notice how your eye wants to keep going, as though it carries on somewhere you can't see. If you pray, let that pull point you toward God; if not, just follow the line.

Image-makers, warned against in a hadith that says they'll be told, on Judgment Day, to breathe life into what they made, and cannot, which is why pattern and word fill a mosque's walls instead. Today's word.
Your line: pattern points past itself. A wall with no faces can still lead the eye somewhere. That's day one thousand five.

1006.title: Geometry without end
1006.hook: stars and interlacing patterns that seem to go on forever
1006.howItsDone: Craftsmen in the Islamic tradition draw geometric patterns with compass and straight edge from a single circle, and set them in tile, wood, plaster and stone across mosques, schools and homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: why no figures in mosques. Ibn Abbas told a worried painter to paint trees, and pattern points past itself.

A compass, the kind with a sharp point and a pencil, from a school pencil case. One circle on a blank page. That's all you start with. From that one circle, with no other tool but a straight edge, craftsmen in Muslim lands drew stars of six and eight and twelve points, bands that weave over and under one another, tiles that lock together and repeat across whole walls and ceilings. Stand in front of one of those walls and your eye can't find where the pattern starts. Today: geometry without end.
screen: `A COMPASS AND ONE CIRCLE.` → `STARS, BANDS, TILES.` → `WHERE DOES IT START?`

segments.voice: These patterns begin with a circle. Open a compass, draw a circle, and without changing the compass, step its point around the edge. It fits exactly six times. Join those points and a six-pointed star appears. Divide the circle another way and you get eight points, or more. From those divisions craftsmen built a grid of lines, and from the grid, stars and polygons. Then they turned the lines into bands and wove them, over, under, over, until the whole surface is one interlacing knot. The Persian name for such patterns is girih, usually rendered a knot. Now the trick that makes them seem endless. The pattern is built as a repeating unit, a tile that fits against copies of itself on every side. So when the wall ends, the pattern doesn't; the edge of the building simply cuts it off. Your eye knows it could go on, past the corner, past the city, forever. What does it mean? The patterns themselves don't say, and Muslims read them in more than one way. Some see the oneness of God: every star, however far out, grows from the same center. Others see the order of creation. The Qur'an invites the reader to look at the heavens God made, to look again and find no flaw, and says that if the sea were ink for the words of God, the sea would run dry before the words did. Others simply see beauty. Every reading meets the same thing: patterns without end.
screen: `IT BEGINS WITH A CIRCLE.` · `STARS FROM THE COMPASS.` · `BANDS WOVEN INTO A KNOT.` · `CUT OFF BY THE WALL, NOT ENDED.` · then, large: `PATTERNS WITHOUT END.`

segments.voice: Draw a circle with a compass, or trace around a cup and mark half its width on a strip of paper to step with. Keeping that same opening, step around the edge from mark to mark until you're back where you began. Join every other mark into a triangle, then the rest into a second triangle, one slow line per breath, and a six-pointed star appears.
Girih. The Persian name for the woven, knotted patterns drawn from a single circle, cut off by the wall but never finished. Today's word.
Your line: patterns without end. The wall stops; the pattern is only cut off. See you tomorrow.

1007.title: The arabesque
1007.hook: endless vines and leaves, growing without beginning or end
1007.howItsDone: Arabesque vines appear in mosque plaster and tile, in the borders of Qur'an manuscripts and on metalwork, often around calligraphy; craftspeople in places such as Iran, Turkey and Morocco still draw and carve them by hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday: girih, the knotted star patterns that run on past the edge of the wall.

A strip of carved plaster runs along the top of a wall, no wider than a hand. A stem curls left, splits, and sends out a leaf. The leaf turns into another stem. That stem curls right, splits again, and sends out half a palm leaf, which turns into yet another stem. Follow it and you never find the root, or the last leaf. At the corner the strip just stops, cut off by its frame, as if the vine carries on behind the plaster. It isn't a picture of a plant from any garden. It's a plant that only grows. Today: the arabesque.
screen: `A STEM CURLS AND SPLITS.` → `NO ROOT, NO LAST LEAF.` → `CUT OFF BY THE FRAME.`

segments.voice: The arabesque turns up in mosque plaster, on palace walls, in the borders of handwritten books, on the lids of metal bowls: stems that split, curl and rejoin, leaves that turn into new stems. Yesterday's geometry was ruled lines and compass circles locking into stars. The arabesque is a living curve. One is crystal; the other is growth. Look at what the artist leaves out. No root to point at, and no flower at the end that says, here, it's finished. Some readers see in it a picture the Qur'an itself draws, a likeness for good speech. In Pickthall's translation: "A goodly saying, as a goodly tree, its root set firm, its branches reaching into heaven." The next verse adds that it gives its fruit at every season, by permission of its Lord. Here the two part ways. The vine on the wall hides its root; the verse insists on one. A good word stands firm underneath, and that's why it can keep bearing fruit above. Nobody can show that an artist carved a vine to illustrate that verse, but it's a fair thing to remember while standing under one. And the vine has a practical gift: it fills any shape. A dome, a window arch, the border of a page of the Qur'an, the lid of a box. The same few moves, stem, split, curl, leaf, can wrap around anything, sometimes around calligraphy, so the words sit inside a garden of their own. Growing without end.
screen: `STEMS THAT SPLIT AND CURL.` · `NO ROOT, NO FINAL FLOWER.` · `A GOODLY SAYING, A GOODLY TREE.` · `IT FILLS ANY SHAPE.` · then, large: `GROWING WITHOUT END.`

segments.voice: In the margin of any page, start a line in the middle, not at the edge, and let it curl. When it wants to, split it in two, give one half a leaf, and let the leaf become a new stem, slowly, without planning and without drawing an ending. If you pray, let each curl carry a quiet remembrance of God; if you don't, just watch the line grow.
The arabesque. A carved or painted vine with no root and no last leaf, curling and splitting to fill any shape. Today's word.
Your line: growing without end. A firm root below, fruit above. Day one thousand seven, done.

1008.title: The dome and the minaret
1008.hook: the dome as the sky, the minaret as the voice
1008.howItsDone: Muslims hear the adhan from minarets, often through loudspeakers now, and pray under domes in many large mosques; plenty of mosques, from storefronts to village prayer rooms, have neither.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the arabesque, a vine with no root and no last leaf, growing without end.

Before the towers, there was a roof. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud tells of a woman whose house stood beside the mosque of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Medina. Hers, she said, was one of the tallest houses around it. Before dawn, Bilal would come, climb up, and sit on her roof, watching for first light. When he saw it, he stood and called the people to prayer. A neighbor's rooftop, a man watching the sky, and a voice. Later, cities would raise towers for that voice, and lift great round roofs over the people praying underneath. Today: the dome and the minaret.
screen: `A NEIGHBOR'S ROOF IN MEDINA.` → `BILAL WATCHES FOR DAWN.` → `A VOICE, THEN A TOWER.`

segments.voice: Take the minaret first, because it is the voice. Its job is to carry the adhan, the call to prayer, over the rooftops: God is greatest, come to prayer, come to success. Minarets take many shapes: square towers in Morocco, the spiral stair you met at Ibn Tulun's mosque, pencil-thin towers in Istanbul. The job is the same: lift a human voice so the whole neighborhood can hear. Today a loudspeaker often does the lifting, and the tower still stands like a finger pointing up: the call comes from here. Now the dome, which is the sky. Stand underneath one and look up. The walls stop being walls and curve over you, gathering toward one point overhead. Inside, a dome may be painted with stars, patterns and verses, like a heaven brought indoors. The Qur'an speaks of God, in Pickthall's words, as the one "Who hath appointed the earth a resting-place for you, and the sky a canopy." A dome is a canopy you can stand under. Put them together and a mosque makes two gestures. The dome gathers people in. The minaret sends a voice out. And neither one is required. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes the Prophet's own mosque as mud brick, with a roof of palm leaves and pillars of palm trunks. A mosque can be a rented room with no dome and no tower. Prayer needs a clean place and a direction. The dome and the minaret are what love for that prayer built on top of it. Sky and voice.
screen: `THE MINARET LIFTS THE CALL.` · `THE DOME IS A SKY INDOORS.` · `ONE GATHERS IN, ONE SENDS OUT.` · `MUD BRICK AND PALM IN MEDINA.` · then, large: `SKY AND VOICE.`

segments.voice: Look up: at a dome if there's one near you, or a ceiling, the open sky, or one you remember with your eyes closed, and rest under the curve. Then listen for any voice calling, near or far. If you pray, you can remember the first words of the call, God is greatest; if you don't, just rest there.
Minaret. The tower that lifts the call to prayer, paired with the dome, a sky you can stand under. Today's word.
Your line: sky and voice. One gathers in, the other sends out. That's the week.
